title: A Hundred Yojanas and No Jewel
story:
Satadhanva rode as though the road were endless and the distance nothing. His mare, Vijnatahridaya, could carry him a hundred yojanas without rest — each yojana a journey of many miles — and behind him came the two men he feared most in the world: Krishna and Balarama of Dwaraka, out to avenge the murder of Satrajit and to recover the Syamantaka jewel.

Days earlier, Satyabhama — Krishna's wife and Satrajit's daughter — had found her father slain in his house in Dwaraka, and the Syamantaka, the great jewel Krishna had once given him, stolen. Every sign pointed to Satadhanva of the Bhoja clan. There was no time for counsel: the moment Krishna was home, he and Balarama mounted their chariot and gave chase, determined to run the killer down before he could reach a friendly court and slip beyond their reach.

The chase carried them out of the Vrishni lands and onto the long roads that led toward Mithila. A hundred yojanas the mare covered, mile after mile, the brothers pressing close behind — farther from Dwaraka than either had ever had cause to ride before. But no creature can outrun exhaustion forever. In a grove on the approach to Mithila, Vijnatahridaya stumbled and stood still, her strength spent and her breath failing; and there rider and horse came to a stop, the chariot closing in behind them.

Krishna looked at the trembling mare, then at his brother. "Wait here," he said. "I will go on foot and take the jewel from him myself." Balarama held the chariot, and Krishna went forward alone, the discus in his hand — the same discus that had ended the lives of demons greater than Satadhanva.

The fugitive had no fight left in him. Krishna overtook him on the edge of Mithila and struck him down with the discus, and the murderer of Satrajit lay dead in the very field where he had hoped to find safety. Krishna bent over the body and searched it; he searched the folds of the fallen man's clothes, and the saddle of the spent mare. There was no jewel. The Syamantaka was not on Satadhanva.

He came back to his brother with empty hands. "Give me the jewel," said Balarama. "I have not got it," Krishna answered. The words fell between the two brothers like a stone. Balarama's face darkened, and his anger rose as it rarely did. "Shame on you," he said, "shame on you. I forgive you because you are my brother — but I will go away from here. I have nothing more to do with you, or with the Vrishnis of Dwaraka." And he turned his back on the chariot and walked into Mithila alone.

King Janaka of Mithila received him with honor, rising from his seat at the sight of his guest and loading him with gifts worthy of a king's affection. Balarama stayed on in Mithila for months, and in that time he found a pupil: Duryodhana, the young prince of Hastinapura, who had come to Janaka's court and received from Balarama the finest instruction in the use of the mace that any teacher could give.

Krishna returned to Dwaraka alone — the murderer punished, the jewel still lost. A pursuit that had begun with a murdered father-in-law had ended with a dead fugitive, a parted brother, and a gem that seemed to have vanished into thin air. But Krishna did not believe in vanishing gems. Somewhere in Dwaraka, someone was keeping a secret about the Syamantaka; and he had already begun to guess whose keeping it had passed into.
reflection: The chase that spans a hundred yojanas ends in nothing: the killer is dead, but the jewel is not on him, and Balarama walks away rather than ride home empty-handed beside his brother. Krishna's pursuit was just, yet justice alone does not return what was stolen — the story turns on the gap between punishing the thief and recovering the loss.
tradition_note: The Bhagavata has Balarama simply go on to Mithila to visit King Janaka, his dearest friend; the Harivamsha presents the parting as a rift, with Balarama angry that Krishna could not produce the jewel. Both agree that Satadhanva was killed near Mithila and that no jewel was found.
next_story_tease: Somewhere in Dwaraka, a secret was being kept about the missing jewel.
hero_scene: Krishna, alone on foot on the road near Mithila, his discus back in his hand, standing over the fallen Satadhanva beside the collapsed mare, while Balarama waits far behind with the chariot.

Balarama waiting with the chariot in the distance
